title: Interfaces, Protocols and Abstract Classes
oneLiner: Inheritance and overriding in one minute, C# interfaces versus Python duck typing and Protocol, abstract classes and ABC, type checks with is and isinstance, and when to use which.
keyTakeaway: An interface is a promise of methods with no code; an abstract class shares code but leaves required gaps. C# checks both at compile time and a class must declare them. Python uses duck typing: any object with the right methods works, Protocol documents that for type checkers, and ABC refuses to create objects with unwritten abstract methods.
explanation:
Code is easier to change when it depends on what an object can do rather than exactly which class it is. A function that sends alarms shouldn't care whether the alarm goes to the screen, an email or a test's list; it only needs something it can call Raise on.

The lesson starts with inheritance, a subclass reusing and overriding a base class's members, because it's the simplest way to get polymorphism: one call that does the right thing for each kind of object.

An interface goes further: it lists the methods a class promises to provide, with no code at all, and any class can sign up. C# makes the promise explicit (class EmailSink : IAlarmSink) and checks it when compiling. Python relies on duck typing: if an object has the method, it works, and if not, the call fails when it runs. Python's Protocol writes the expectation down for type checkers without changing that.

An abstract class sits in between: real shared code and data, plus abstract members that every subclass must fill in, and no objects of the abstract class itself. Python builds these with ABC and @abstractmethod. The lesson ends with a table of which to reach for. The Software Design & OOP section takes these ideas further.
